sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Detailed specimen preparation procedures fall to CEN/TC 341, based on those recommended by ISSMGE European Technical Committee 5 on laboratory testing (ETC 5); this annex gives the main requirements.
sections.body: (1) Detailed procedures are in the scope of CEN/TC 341, based on the test procedures recommended by the European Technical Committee 5 on "Laboratory Testing" (ETC 5) of the International Society of Soil Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering; this annex gives the main requirements. (p. 143)
key_points: Detailed procedures: CEN/TC 341, based on ISSMGE ETC 5 (p. 143).

sections.title: Drying of soil
sections.summary: Soil should normally be tested in its natural state without drying; where drying is needed use oven drying to constant mass at (105 ± 5) °C, partial oven drying below 100 °C, or partial air drying at room temperature.
sections.body: (1) Unless otherwise specified, soil should not be dried before testing but used in its natural state. Where drying is necessary use one of: oven drying to constant mass in a ventilated oven at (105 ± 5) °C; oven drying in a ventilated oven at a specified temperature below 100 °C (partial drying, which need not be complete at the lower temperature); air drying (partial) at room temperature, with or without a fan. (p. 143)
key_points: Normally test soil in its natural state (p. 143).
Oven drying to constant mass at (105 ± 5) °C (p. 143).
Partial drying below 100 °C or in air at room temperature (p. 143).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Disaggregating
sections.summary: Specify the extent of disaggregation and treatment of cemented material, done at natural water content, breaking aggregations without crushing particles: no more severe than a rubber-headed pestle, extra care with friable particles, large quantities in batches.
sections.body: (1) The extent of disaggregating and the treatment of any remaining cemented material should suit the specific requirements and conditions and be specified; in particular both should be done at the natural water content. (2) Break aggregations down without crushing individual particles, with action no more severe than a rubber-headed pestle; take special care with friable particles, and disaggregate large quantities in batches. (p. 143)
key_points: Disaggregate at the natural water content (p. 143).
No more severe than a rubber-headed pestle (p. 143).
Large quantities in batches (p. 143).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Subdividing
sections.summary: Mix disaggregated soil thoroughly before subdividing, and repeat the subdivision until representative samples of the specified minimum masses are obtained.
sections.body: (1) Mix the disaggregated soil thoroughly before subdividing, and repeat the subdivision until representative samples of the specified minimum masses are obtained for use as test specimens. (p. 143)
key_points: Mix thoroughly, then subdivide to representative minimum masses (p. 143).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Mass of disturbed soil for testing
sections.summary: Table L.1 gives minimum masses of disturbed soil for each test, some tied to the minimum mass for sieving (MMS) of Table L.2; the masses allow one specimen with some wastage but no over-size particles, and removed oversize material should be recorded.
sections.body: (1) Table L.1 summarises the minimum masses of disturbed soil required for testing; where the minimum mass depends on the largest particles present in significant quantity it is related to the minimum mass for sieving (MMS) of Table L.2 (p. 143). (2) The Table L.1 masses allow for one test specimen with some wastage, not for over-size particles; where only the fine fraction is tested, the prepared sample of the original soil should be large enough to give the specified mass of that fraction. (3) Where large particles are removed to prepare specimens, record the size range and the proportion by dry mass of the oversize material removed (p. 144). (pp. 143 to 144)
key_points: Minimum masses of disturbed soil in Table L.1 (p. 143).
MMS: minimum mass for sieving, Table L.2 (p. 143).
Masses allow one specimen with some wastage (p. 144).
Record size range and dry-mass proportion of removed oversize material (p. 144).

sections.title: Preparation of soil for compaction
sections.summary: Soil for compaction-related tests should not dry, any water reduction being by air drying; particles larger than the Table L.3 limit for the mould (20 mm one-litre mould and CBR determination, 37,5 mm CBR mould) should be removed first.
sections.body: (1) Soil for compaction-related tests should not be allowed to dry; any reduction of water content should be by air drying (p. 144). (2) The upper limit of allowable particle size depends on the mould; remove larger particles before preparing the soil for testing (see Table L.3) (p. 145). (pp. 144 to 145)
key_points: Do not let compaction soil dry; reduce water by air drying (p. 144).
Remove particles above the Table L.3 limits for the mould (p. 145).

sections.title: Preparation of undisturbed specimens
sections.summary: Preparation of specimens from undisturbed samples depends on the sample and specimen type; Table L.4 gives the approximate mass for typical specimens, enough for one specimen with some trimming wastage.
sections.body: (1) The method of preparing specimens from undisturbed samples depends on the type of sample and of specimen. (2) Table L.4 gives the approximate mass for typical laboratory specimens, sufficient for one specimen with some allowance for trimming wastage. (p. 145)
key_points: Method depends on sample and specimen type (p. 145).
Table L.4 gives approximate masses for undisturbed specimens (p. 145).

sections.title: Preparation of re-compacted specimens
sections.summary: Heading for preparation of re-compacted specimens; the text sits in its sub-clauses L.4.1 to L.4.5.
sections.body: Heading for L.4.1 to L.4.5; it has no text of its own. (p. 145)

sections.title: General requirements
sections.summary: Re-compact disturbed soil to a specified compactive effort or a specified dry density at a specified water content; clay should not dry (water added is mixed in and stands sealed at least 24 hours), soil is broken down first, oversize removed per Table L.5, and grading checked before and after.
sections.body: (1) Disturbed soil may be re-compacted into specimens to either criterion: a specified compactive effort at a specified water content, or a specified dry density at a specified water content (p. 145). (2) Clay soil to be re-compacted should not be allowed to dry; reduce water content by air drying; added water should be well mixed in and the soil left in a sealed container for at least 24 hours before use. (3) Break the soil down before re-compaction. (4) The upper limit of allowable particle size depends on the specimen size; remove particles larger than those in Table L.5 (p. 146). (5) Check the particle size distribution of a re-compacted specimen before and after compaction (p. 147). Tables L.2 to L.5 are printed within this clause, pp. 145 to 147. (pp. 145 to 147)
key_points: Specified compactive effort or specified dry density, at a specified water content (p. 145).
Added water: mix and store sealed at least 24 hours (p. 146).
Particle size limits in Table L.5: H/5, H/10, d/5, d/12 (p. 147).
Check grading before and after compaction (p. 147).
tables: Table L.2: Minimum mass for sieving - largest particle diameter (D), mm; minimum mass for sieving (MMS): 75, 120 kg; 63, 70 kg; 45, 25 kg; 37,5, 15 kg; 31,5, 10 kg; 22,4, 4 kg; 20, 2 kg; 16, 1,5 kg; 11,2, 600 g; 10, 500 g; 8, 400 g; 5,6, 250 g; 4, 200 g; 2,8, 150 g; ≤ 2, 100 g (p. 145)

sections.title: Re-compacted sample larger than test specimen
sections.summary: For oedometer, direct shear or compressive strength specimens, compact soil in a larger mould, extrude it and trim as for undisturbed samples (not suitable for granular soil); permeability specimens may be compacted in the test mould; clayey compacted samples cure sealed at least 24 h.
sections.body: (1) For oedometer consolidation, direct shear or compressive strength specimens, normally compact the soil in the specified manner into a mould larger than the desired specimen, extrude it and prepare the specimen by the procedures for undisturbed samples. NOTE: the method is not suitable for granular soil. (2) Permeability specimens may be compacted directly into the mould or container of the test. (3) For a specified effort, the compactive effort should normally correspond to one of the two compaction test types (see 5.10 and Annex R), applied in layers with the top of each lightly scarified before the next. (4) For a specified density, compact dynamically or compress under a static load, weighing and measuring volume after each layer; preliminary trials may help choose the method. (5) If clay is present, seal and store the compacted sample for a curing period of at least 24 h before extrusion. (p. 147)
key_points: Compact in a larger mould, extrude and trim (p. 147).
Not suitable for granular soil (p. 147).
Layers with each top lightly scarified (p. 147).
Clayey samples cure sealed at least 24 h (p. 147).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Re-compaction of test specimen
sections.summary: Small direct shear, oedometer or compressive strength specimens are tamped, kneaded or compacted into the mould, ring or tube (hand rammer, Harvard apparatus or kneading), avoiding cavities, with the procedure found by trial and recorded; 100 mm or larger cylinders may use a compaction rammer.
sections.body: (1) For small direct shear, oedometer or compressive strength specimens, tamp, knead or compact the soil into the mould, ring or tube, using a suitable hand rammer, the Harvard compaction apparatus or a kneading action, avoiding cavities; determine the exact procedure for the desired density or compactive effort by trial and record it so it can be repeated for specimens of consistent properties (p. 147). (2) Cylindrical specimens of 100 mm diameter or more may be compacted with a compaction rammer, with the number of layers and blows per layer specified. (3) If clay is present, seal and store the compacted specimen for at least 24 h before use, so excess pore water pressures dissipate (p. 148). (pp. 147 to 148)
key_points: Hand rammer, Harvard compaction apparatus or kneading (p. 147).
Find the procedure by trial and record it (p. 147).
100 mm or larger: compaction rammer, layers and blows specified (p. 148).
Clayey specimens cure sealed at least 24 h (p. 148).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Re-saturation
sections.summary: A re-compacted specimen is initially unsaturated and normally needs re-saturation before testing by a recognised method from the shear strength or compressibility test procedures, confirmed by the B value where applicable.
sections.body: (1) A re-compacted specimen will invariably be initially unsaturated; re-saturation is normally needed before testing, by one of the recognised saturation methods of the shear strength or compressibility test procedures, with full saturation confirmed by checking the B value, if applicable. (p. 148)
key_points: Re-saturate by a recognised method (p. 148).
Confirm full saturation by the B value (p. 148).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Remoulded test specimen
sections.summary: Remould soil sealed in a plastic bag by squeezing and kneading with the fingers for several minutes, then work it into the mould, e.g. with a tamping rod, quickly and without trapping air, then extrude and trim.
sections.body: (1) Remoulding can be done by sealing the soil in a plastic bag and squeezing and kneading it with the fingers for several minutes; form the specimen by working the soil into the mould, e.g. with a tamping rod, as quickly as possible to avoid change of water content and without entrapping air; then extrude and trim. (p. 148)
key_points: Knead in a sealed plastic bag for several minutes (p. 148).
Work quickly without entrapping air (p. 148).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Preparation of reconstituted specimens
sections.summary: Heading for preparation of reconstituted specimens; the text sits in its sub-clauses L.5.1 to L.5.3.
sections.body: Heading for L.5.1 to L.5.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 148)

sections.title: Preparation of slurry
sections.summary: Mix soil with water into a homogeneous pourable slurry above the liquid limit, about twice the liquid limit usually, preferably from natural water content without drying or grinding; wet sieve coarser particles if needed, with distilled, de-ionized or suitable water.
sections.body: (1) Mix the soil thoroughly with water into a homogeneous slurry with water content above the liquid limit, preferably starting from the natural water content without drying, since drying and grinding to powder may change its properties; coarser particles can be removed by wet sieving if necessary; the mixing water may be distilled or de-ionized, or of the appropriate chemistry; the slurry should be fluid enough to pour, about twice the liquid limit usually being satisfactory. (p. 148)
key_points: Slurry above the liquid limit, usually about twice wL (p. 148).
Avoid drying and grinding (p. 148).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Consolidation
sections.summary: Consolidate the slurry in a cell large enough for the specimen, drained without losing particles: first under the top plate alone until the ends stiffen, then under a vertical stress enough for handling, held until consolidation is substantially complete.
sections.body: (1) The cell should be large enough to give a test specimen, or a sample for trimming, of the required size after consolidation, with drainage provided without letting soil particles escape. (2) After pouring, apply initial consolidation under the weight of the top plate only until the ends stiffen enough to prevent loss of material under further loading; the consolidation stress should allow handling when consolidated and be kept long enough for consolidation to be substantially complete. (p. 148)
key_points: Drained cell large enough for the specimen (p. 148).
Top plate weight first, then a handling stress until consolidation is complete (p. 148).
sections.applicability: Detailed specimen-preparation procedures underlying every soil laboratory test in Section 5.

sections.title: Specimen preparation
sections.summary: Extrude the consolidated sample from the cell and trim it to specimens; one-dimensional consolidation tests may be run in the cell used to consolidate the slurry.
sections.body: (1) Extrude the consolidated sample from the cell and trim as necessary for test specimens. (2) One-dimensional consolidation tests on the reconstituted soil may be carried out in the cell in which it was consolidated from slurry. (p. 149)
key_points: Extrude and trim (p. 149).
Oedometer tests may use the consolidation cell (p. 149).

sections.title: Checklists for classification testing
sections.summary: The number of classification specimens depends on soil variability and experience; Table M.1 suggests minimum numbers per stratum (e.g. particle size 4-6 without and 2-4 with comparable experience) and Table M.2 gives a checklist for each classification test.
sections.body: (1) The number of specimens depends on the variability of the soil and the experience with it, and to a lesser extent than other soil tests on the geotechnical problem; Table M.1 gives guidance on the number of classification tests. (2) Table M.2 gives a checklist for each soil classification test in the document (p. 150). NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1 (p. 151). (pp. 150 to 151)
key_points: Table M.1: minimum samples per stratum by comparable experience (p. 150).
Particle size distribution 4-6 (no experience), 2-4 (with) (p. 150).
Fall cone method recommended for the liquid limit (p. 151).
tables: Table M.1: Classification tests. Suggested minimum number of samples to be tested in one soil stratum - classification test; comparable experience no, yes: particle size distribution 4-6, 2-4; water content all samples of Quality Class 1 to 3; strength index test all samples of Quality Class 1; consistency limits (Atterberg limits) 3-5, 1-3; loss on ignition (for organic and clay soil) 3-5, 1-3; bulk density every element test; density index as appropriate; particle density 2, 1; carbonate content, sulfate content, pH, chloride content, soil dispersibility, frost susceptibility as appropriate (p. 150)

Table M.2: Checklist for soil classification tests - water content: check sample storage; coordinate with other classification tests; standard oven-drying not appropriate for gypsum or organic soil, precautions may be needed; report gypsum or organic soil; coarse soil may need correction of measured water content; correction needed for saline soil (p. 150); bulk density: select test method; check sampling and handling; large earthwork projects may need an adapted or field method; sands and gravels may need correction of measured density; particle density: oven-dried versus moist preparation can influence results; check for enclosed pores, special techniques may suit, report them; results outside typical values call for more determinations, mineralogy and organic content affect results; particle size analysis: method depends on particle size and gradation; carbonates and organic matter influence results, remove them if appropriate or adapt the method; check correct quartering; consistency limits (Atterberg limits): select the liquid limit method, several acceptable but fall cone recommended; check storage, preparation (homogenisation and mixing) and whether drying was used; drying can influence results dramatically and oven drying should be avoided; test oxidising soil quickly; results need not be reliable for thixotropic soil; density index for granular soil: check storage; select test type; results very dependent on procedure; prepared specimens highly non-uniform; soil dispersibility: consider different compaction conditions for specimens; avoid drying before testing; select procedures; run classification tests in addition; frost susceptibility: - (p. 151)

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Dissolved salts in saline pore water stay after drying and distort the water content, so the fluid content (water plus salts per unit mass of dry soil) may suit better; laboratory water content of coarse soil limited by sample size should be corrected for the oversize grains.
sections.body: (1) In saline soil the dissolved salts remain after drying and may give an incorrect water content; the fluid content, the mass of fluid (water plus salts) per unit mass of dry soil, may be more appropriate. (2) For a coarse soil whose maximum grain diameter in the laboratory sample is limited by the sample size, the laboratory water content may differ from the in place value; correct it as a function of the percentage of grains larger than the maximum grain diameter. NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1.2. (p. 152)
key_points: Saline soil: fluid content may be more appropriate (p. 152).
Correct coarse-soil water content for oversize grains (p. 152).

sections.summary: Heading for bulk density determination; the text sits in its sub-clauses M.3.1 and M.3.2.

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: The linear measurement method suits fine soil only; coarse soil density comes from in-situ tests or, more accurately, frozen undisturbed samples; Table M.3 sets 1 to 4 density tests per clay or silty stratum by density range and experience.
sections.body: (1) The linear measurement method is appropriate for fine soil only; for coarse soil density can normally be found with sufficient accuracy from in-situ tests, and more accurately from measurements on a frozen "undisturbed" sample. (2) Table M.3 guides the minimum number of tests for one stratum of clay or silty soil; a single test represents a verification of existing knowledge. NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1.3. (p. 152)
key_points: Linear measurement method for fine soil only (p. 152).
Coarse soil: in-situ tests or frozen samples (p. 152).
Range ≥ 0,02 Mg/m3: 4, 3, 2 tests by experience (p. 152).
tables: Table M.3: Density tests. Minimum number of soil specimens to be tested for one soil stratum - variability in measured density; comparable experience none, medium, extensive: range of measured density ≥ 0,02 Mg/m3 4, 3, 2; range of measured density ≤ 0,02 Mg/m3 3, 2, 1 (p. 152)
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural checklists and minimum test counts for the routine soil classification/identification/description test suite of 5.5.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Check bulk density results by the degree of saturation, not above 100 %; laboratory dry density of coarse soil limited by sample size should be corrected for grains above the maximum diameter.
sections.body: (1) Check the results by calculating the degree of saturation, which should not exceed 100 %. (2) For a coarse soil whose maximum grain diameter in the laboratory sample is limited by the sample size, the dry density may differ from the in place value; correct it as a function of the percentage of grains larger than the maximum grain diameter. (p. 152)
key_points: Degree of saturation should not exceed 100 % (p. 152).
Correct coarse-soil dry density for oversize grains (p. 152).

sections.title: Particle density determination
sections.summary: Particle density needs little material (minimum 10 g below 4 mm), usually from another test's specimen; enclosed pores give only an apparent density unless ground or tested specially; organic soil needs special procedures; He-pycnometer and other modern methods are calibrated against common ones.
sections.body: (1) The material needed is very small (minimum of 10 g with particle size less than 4 mm), usually taken from a specimen used for another laboratory test. (2) In porous materials with enclosed pores the particles have only an apparent density; the solid density may be found by finely grinding the specimens, the closed pore volume by water saturation or gas pressure techniques in specialised laboratories, then measuring the solid particle density by a special technique. (3) Soil with organic materials should be tested by special procedures, otherwise the values should be used with caution. (4) Modern methods such as the He-pycnometer may be applied, calibrated against a more common method such as those in X.4.1.4. NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1.4. (p. 153)
key_points: Minimum 10 g with particles below 4 mm (p. 153).
Enclosed pores give an apparent density only (p. 153).
Calibrate the He-pycnometer against common methods (p. 153).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural checklists and minimum test counts for the routine soil classification/identification/description test suite of 5.5.

sections.title: Particle size analysis
sections.summary: Coarse soil is sieved after washing, fine soil by sedimentation including sieving sand-sized particles, mixed soil by both; clays and organic soil need care since drying at 105 °C may cement clay irreversibly or oxidise organic matter; X-ray, laser and similar methods are calibrated against these.
sections.body: (1) For coarse soil (predominantly gravel and/or sand sizes) the particle size distribution is determined by sieving after washing, sedimentation not usually being needed; for fine soil (predominantly silt and/or clay sizes) the sedimentation procedure is used, including sieving any sand-sized particles; for mixed soil both are used. (2) Take special care with clays and organic soil: clay particles may have a cementing effect that can become irreversible on drying at 105 °C, and organic matter partly oxidises at 105 °C. (3) Modern methods with X-ray, laser beam, density measurement or particle counter detection may be applied, calibrated against the methods in (2) (as printed). NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1.5. (p. 153)
key_points: Coarse soil: sieving after washing (p. 153).
Fine soil: sedimentation with sieving of sand-sized particles (p. 153).
Drying at 105 °C can cement clay or oxidise organic matter (p. 153).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural checklists and minimum test counts for the routine soil classification/identification/description test suite of 5.5.

sections.title: Density index test of granular soil
sections.summary: Density index of granular soil: at least two specimens per stratum for maximum density and three for minimum density.
sections.body: (1) The recommended minimum number of specimens for one stratum is two for the maximum density and three for the minimum density. NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1.7. (p. 153)
key_points: Two specimens for maximum density, three for minimum density (p. 153).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Some natural clayey soils disperse rapidly in slow-moving water by colloidal erosion along cracks and flow channels, making them highly susceptible to erosion and piping; dispersive clays are usually high in sodium.
sections.body: (1) Some natural clayey soils disperse rapidly in slow moving water by colloidal erosion along cracks or other flow channels and are highly susceptible to erosion and piping; the tendency depends on the mineralogy and chemistry of the clay and the dissolved salts in the pore water and eroding water; dispersive clays are usually high sodium content soil. (p. 154)
key_points: Dispersive soils are highly susceptible to erosion and piping (p. 154).
Dispersive clays usually have high sodium content (p. 154).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural checklists and minimum test counts for the routine soil classification/identification/description test suite of 5.5.

sections.title: Test procedures for all tests
sections.summary: Dispersibility tests do not apply to soil with less than 10 % clay and plasticity index ≤ 4 %; minimum specimens per stratum: two each for pinhole, double hydrometer and soluble salts tests and three for the crumb test, by engineering judgement.
sections.body: (1) Dispersibility tests are not applicable to soil with clay content of less than 10 % and plasticity index less than or equal to 4 %. (2) The recommended minimum number of specimens for one stratum is two for the pinhole test, two for the double hydrometer test, two for the soluble salts in pore water test and three for the crumb test; base the number of tests on engineering judgement. NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1.8. (p. 154)
key_points: Not applicable below 10 % clay with Ip ≤ 4 % (p. 154).
Pinhole, double hydrometer, soluble salts: two each; crumb test: three (p. 154).

sections.title: Pinhole test
sections.summary: Pinhole test per X.4.1.8 except: compact in a Harvard miniature mould near the plastic limit, five layers for (38 ± 2) mm, to 95 % of standard maximum dry density; report classification, density, heads and times, flow rates, cloudiness, hole size and shape, and soil class.
sections.body: (1) Follow the literature in X.4.1.8, except that: the specimen is compacted in a Harvard miniature mould at a water content close to the plastic limit; five layers make up the total height of (38 ± 2) mm; a constant effort per layer gives a dry density equal to 95 % of the maximum dry density from standard compaction test(s). (2) Present: the classification test results; the specimen density; the water heads used and testing time under each; the flow rates through the specimen; the cloudiness of the flowing fluid at the end of the test; the hole size and shape after test; the soil classification by standard reference. NOTE: examples of methods are in the documents listed in X.4.1.8. (p. 154)
key_points: Harvard miniature mould near the plastic limit (p. 154).
Five layers, (38 ± 2) mm, at 95 % of maximum dry density (p. 154).
Report heads, times, flow rates, cloudiness, hole size and shape (p. 154).

sections.summary: The double hydrometer test reports grain size curves with and without dispersant and mechanical shaking or stirring, and the percentage dispersion.
sections.body: (1) Present the grain size curves obtained with and without a dispersant solution and mechanical shaking/stirring, and the percentage dispersion. (p. 154)
key_points: Curves with and without dispersant; percentage dispersion (p. 154).

sections.title: Crumb test
sections.summary: The crumb test reports the soil classification as dispersive or non-dispersive and details of the reagent used.
sections.body: (1) Present the soil classification as dispersive or non-dispersive and details of the reagent used. NOTE: examples of such classifications are in the documents listed in X.4.1.8. (p. 155)
key_points: Dispersive or non-dispersive, with the reagent used (p. 155).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Frost heave specimens: natural samples unfrozen in soft clayey and silty soil or frozen in clay, silt and sand, at least five times the maximum grain size and 75 mm; reconstituted at least 100 mm; back-pressure saturation allowed; CBR near optimum water content, several tests for variations.
sections.body: (1) A natural-state sample can be obtained unfrozen in soft clayey and silty soil or frozen in clay, silt and sand (without gravel), and reshaped carefully if needed. (2) A sample to be re-compacted can be strongly remoulded provided sampling has not altered its grain size distribution. (3) A natural specimen should be at least five times the maximum grain size in diameter and no less than 75 mm; a reconstituted specimen at least 100 mm. (4) Both may be saturated with back-pressure before the frost heave test. (5) A CBR test, if needed, is made on a specimen compacted close to the optimum water content from a compaction test. (6) Generally one CBR test is made per sample, but several should be made to assess the influence of, for example, water content variations and compactive force. NOTE: examples of procedures and of evaluations based on index tests are in the documents listed in X.4.1.9 and X.5. (p. 155)
key_points: Natural specimen ≥ 5 × maximum grain size and ≥ 75 mm (p. 155).
Reconstituted specimen ≥ 100 mm (p. 155).
CBR near optimum water content (p. 155).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural checklists and minimum test counts for the routine soil classification/identification/description test suite of 5.5.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: A soil is frost-susceptible if it shows segregational heaving in the laboratory frost heave test; in clayey low-permeability soils longer winters, from altitude and latitude, make frost action more severe, notably in northern and alpine countries.
sections.body: (1) A soil is deemed frost-susceptible if it exhibits segregational heaving in the laboratory frost heave test (p. 155). (2) In clayey soils of low permeability the degree of frost action depends on the length of the winter, i.e. the altitude and latitude of the site; the longer the winter the more severe the action, to be taken into account in northern and alpine countries (p. 156). (pp. 155 to 156)
key_points: Frost-susceptible: segregational heaving in the frost heave test (p. 155).
Longer winters, more severe frost action in clayey soils (p. 156).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: The routine chemical tests are traditional laboratory methods, other substances going to specialist laboratories; 100 g of dry soil suffices for most tests; store at 5 °C to 10 °C where possible; calibrate with blind and reference samples and report any procedural deviations with reasons.
sections.body: (1) The routine chemical tests rest on traditional methods within the capability of many geotechnical laboratories; tests for other substances should normally go to a specialist chemical laboratory. (2) One hundred grams of dry soil is sufficient for most chemical testing; a much larger dried sample is usually needed at the outset, and thorough mixing and correct sub-dividing are essential. (3) Storage temperature may influence biological degradation of organic matter; keep chemical test material at 5 °C to 10 °C whenever possible. (4) Most methods include calibration with "blind" and reference samples; electrochemical methods like pH use solutions of known pH. (5) Special requirements may call for deviations from standard procedures, including specimen preparation; report any deviations clearly with the reasons. NOTE: examples for the five chemical tests are in the documents listed in X.4.2; equivalent methods exist in other national standards and textbooks. (p. 157)
key_points: 100 g of dry soil suffices for most chemical testing (p. 157).
Store at 5 °C to 10 °C where possible (p. 157).
Report procedural deviations with reasons (p. 157).

sections.title: Number of tests
sections.summary: Organic, carbonate and sulfate content, pH and chloride content can vary widely within one stratum, so multiple tests on closely-spaced samples may be needed to define local variability.
sections.body: (1) The number of tests should allow for organic content, carbonate content, sulfate content, pH value and chloride content varying widely even within a geological stratum; multiple tests on closely-spaced samples may be necessary to define the local variability. (p. 157)
key_points: Chemical properties vary widely within a stratum (p. 157).
Closely-spaced multiple tests may be needed (p. 157).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Loss on ignition on soil finer than 2 mm assumes all mass lost is burnt organic matter, which holds only with little clay or carbonate; dry at (50 ± 2,5) °C rather than (105 ± 5) °C; ignite at (440 ± 25) °C, 500 °C or 520 °C mostly suiting, minding clay, gypsum, sulfide and carbonate breakdown.
sections.body: (1) Loss on ignition is normally determined on a representative sample finer than 2 mm as the mass lost on ignition at the specified temperature, assuming the organic mass burns totally and causes all the loss (p. 157). (2) It relates to organic content in soil with little or no clay and carbonates; with more clay and/or carbonate, unrelated factors could cause most of the loss. (3) A drying temperature below the usual (105 ± 5) °C is needed to avoid oxidising organic matter; the examples in X.4.2.2 specify (50 ± 2,5) °C, which might not remove all water, and trials may be needed. (4) The examples in (1) specify ignition at (440 ± 25) °C, other standards up to 900 °C; specify with caution since some clay minerals begin to disintegrate at about 550 °C, chemically-bound water may go at lower temperatures (from 200 °C in some clay minerals; gypsum disintegrates from about 65 °C), and sulfide may oxidise and carbonates disintegrate at 650 °C to 900 °C; for most purposes 500 °C or 520 °C is appropriate. (5) Drying and ignition periods should reach equilibrium; with ignition under 3 h the report should document constant mass confirmed by repeated weighing. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.2.2 (p. 158). (pp. 157 to 158)
key_points: Loss on ignition on soil finer than 2 mm (p. 157).
Ignition (440 ± 25) °C in the examples; 500 °C or 520 °C for most purposes (p. 158).
Clay minerals from about 550 °C; gypsum from about 65 °C (p. 158).
Ignition under 3 h: confirm constant mass (p. 158).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Loss on ignition relates to organic carbon and matter only if corrected for other expelled constituents; direct measurement of organic carbon avoids its errors.
sections.body: (1) Organic carbon and organic matter can be related to loss on ignition if it is corrected for other expelled constituents. (2) Direct measurement of the organic carbon content avoids the errors of the loss on ignition method. (p. 158)
key_points: Correct loss on ignition for other expelled constituents (p. 158).
Direct organic carbon measurement avoids its errors (p. 158).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Rapid titration is the preferred carbonate method for this standard, accurate enough for soil if dissolution is finished and enough duplicates are run; gasometer measurement of liberated CO2 under controlled temperature and pressure is an alternative (X.4.2.3).
sections.body: (1) Examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.2.3; for this standard the rapid titration method is preferred, accurate enough for soil provided the dissolution is finalised and sufficient duplicate tests are made. (2) Other examples in X.4.2.3 measure the liberated carbon dioxide (CO2) in a gasometer under controlled temperature and atmospheric pressure. (p. 158)
key_points: Rapid titration preferred (p. 158).
Finish dissolution; run sufficient duplicates (p. 158).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Carbonate content expressed as CO2 is formally correct but impractical, so results may be given as equivalent calcium carbonate: CaCO3 = 2,273 • CO2, both as percentage of dry weight.
sections.body: (1) Expressing the carbonate content as the amount of CO2 is formally correct but impractical for design; results may be given as equivalent calcium carbonate CaCO3, the carbonate composition for most soil types, from CaCO3 = 2,273 • CO2, CaCO3 and CO2 contents as percentage of dry weight. (p. 159)
key_points: Both as percentage of dry weight (p. 159).

equations.description: CaCO3 = 2,273 • CO2; CaCO3 and CO2 contents as percentage of dry weight (p. 159)

sections.title: Test Procedures
sections.summary: The gravimetric method on acid or water extract or groundwater is preferred unless an alternative is shown as accurate; dry gypsum at 50 °C, since above about 65 °C it loses crystal water; SO4 2- = 1,2 SO3 2-, both as percentages.
sections.body: (1) The gravimetric method for acid or water extract or groundwater is the preferred one, unless parallel analysis shows an alternative of equal or better accuracy. (2) Gypsum (CaSO4 • 2H2O) should be dried at 50 °C; gypsum-bearing samples lose water of crystallisation above about 65 °C, which can give erroneously high measured water contents. (3) SO4 2- = 1,2 SO3 2-, with SO3 2- and SO4 2- contents as percentages. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.2.4. (p. 159)
key_points: Gravimetric method preferred (p. 159).
Dry gypsum at 50 °C; water loss above about 65 °C (p. 159).

equations.description: SO4 2- = 1,2 SO3 2-, with SO3 2- and SO4 2- contents expressed as a percentage (p. 159)

sections.applicability: Detailed chemical-test procedures and the standard unit conversions for reporting carbonate and sulfate content.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Calcium sulfate is poorly soluble but appreciable amounts dissolve over geological time, as in karst; take care with marginal results; sulfides and sesquioxides affect the reactions, and sulfides can oxidise to more sulfate.
sections.body: (1) Interpret allowing that calcium sulfate solubility is low but appreciable quantities can dissolve over geological time, as in karstic formations; take particular care when results are marginal to classification categories. (2) Other substances, notably sulfides and sesquioxides, can affect the reactions and so the results; sulfides can oxidise in the long term to produce additional sulfates. (p. 159)
key_points: Care with results marginal to classification categories (p. 159).
Sulfides can oxidise to additional sulfates (p. 159).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Of the methods for pH, the electrometric method reading pH directly in a soil suspension or groundwater is recommended as definitive.
sections.body: (1) Several methods exist; the electrometric method, a direct reading in a prepared soil suspension or in groundwater, is recommended as the definitive method. (p. 160)
key_points: Electrometric method is definitive (p. 160).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Erroneous pH results come from missing or wrong meter calibration before and after each set, poorly protected electrodes, readings before the meter stabilises, and poorly washed groundwater containers.
sections.body: (1) Erroneous results can be caused by: omitting or wrong calibration of the pH meter before and after each set of tests; inadequate protection of electrodes when not in use; reading before the meter is stable; contamination from inadequately washed groundwater sampling containers. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.2.5. (p. 160)
key_points: Calibrate the pH meter before and after each set (p. 160).
Wait for a stable reading (p. 160).

sections.summary: Heading for chloride content determination; the text sits in its sub-clauses N.6.1 and N.6.2.

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Chloride by Mohr's method (water-soluble), Volhard's method (acid- or water-soluble) or electrochemical conductivity; a quick silver nitrate turbidity test confirms chlorides; Volhard back-titrates excess silver nitrate with potassium thiocyanate; Mohr titrates with 0,02 N silver nitrate and suits groundwater.
sections.body: (1) Procedures include Mohr's method for water-soluble chlorides, Volhard's method for acid-soluble or water-soluble chlorides, and electrochemical procedures. (2) The first two use the exchange reaction between chlorides and silver nitrate with different analyses, both needing careful observation and weighing; the third measures conductivity in dilutions of known water content. (3) A quick qualitative test: about 5 ml of filtered groundwater or 1:1 soil-water extract in a test-tube, acidified with a few drops of nitric acid if highly alkaline (pH 12-14), then a few drops of 1 % silver nitrate solution; appreciable turbidity shows chlorides in measurable quantity. (4) Volhard's method underlies 7.2 (water-soluble) and 7.3 (acid-soluble chlorides) of BS 1377-3:1990 and BS 812-118:1988 for mineral aggregates: excess silver nitrate is added to the acidified solution and the unreacted portion back-titrated with potassium thiocyanate, with ferric aluminium as indicator. (5) In Mohr's method the test solution and a blank are each titrated with 0,02 N silver nitrate, potassium chromate as indicator; it is preferable for chlorides in groundwater (p. 160). NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.2.6 (p. 161). (pp. 160 to 161)
key_points: Mohr, Volhard or electrochemical methods (p. 160).
Quick test: 1 % silver nitrate turbidity (p. 160).
Mohr's method, 0,02 N silver nitrate, preferable for groundwater (p. 160).

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Because the chloride anion is very mobile, the theoretical link between salinity as sodium chloride content and chloride content need not hold.
sections.body: (1) The theoretical relationship between salinity expressed as sodium chloride content and chloride content need not hold, due to the very mobile nature of the chloride anion. (p. 161)
key_points: Salinity and chloride content need not correspond (p. 161).

sections.title: Detailed information on strength index testing of soil
sections.summary: Table O.1 gives a summary checklist for strength index tests on clayey soil: any test gives only an approximate, uncertain index affected by testing rate; the laboratory vane adds sensitivity and remoulded strength; the fall cone needs cone wear and tip angle checks.
sections.body: (1) Table O.1 suggests a summary checklist on the procedures for the strength index tests for soil in this standard. NOTE: examples of procedures for the laboratory vane and fall cone tests are in the documents listed in X.4.3. (p. 162)
key_points: Strength index tests give an approximate, uncertain index of shear strength (p. 162).
Results depend on testing rate; check repeatability (p. 162).
Fall cone: check cone tip wear and angle (p. 162).
tables: Table O.1: Checklist for strength index tests on clayey soil - any strength index test: tests provide an approximate index of shear strength; large uncertainty in the measurements; use results cautiously for non-homogeneous and jointed/slickensided soil; all results affected by the applied testing rate; test repeatability needs checking; laboratory vane: also measures sensitivity and remoulded shear strength; check mode of rotation (hand-operated versus motorised); tests on extruded samples or in sampling tube; fall cone: tests on extruded samples or in sampling tube on intact material, supplemented with a test on remoulded material to establish the sensitivity, the ratio of intact to remoulded strength; also measures sensitivity on remoulded specimen; check wear on tip of cone; check tip cone angle (p. 162)

sections.title: Number of tests
sections.summary: Table P.1 sets minimum triaxial tests per stratum by variability and experience: for φ' by correlation coefficient r (4, 3, 2 tests at r ≤ 0,95), for cu by max/min ratio (6, 4, 3 above 2), each test a set of three specimens; fewer tests if field data exist.
sections.body: (1) Table P.1 guides the minimum number of tests as a function of soil variability and comparable experience; if only one test set is required it verifies existing knowledge, and more tests should be run if new results disagree with existing data. (2) The number may be reduced if shear stress data are available from other methods, for example field tests. NOTE: examples of procedures are in X.4.4. (p. 163)
key_points: φ': r ≤ 0,95 needs 4, 3, 2 tests by experience (p. 163).
cu: max/min ratio > 2 needs 6, 4, 3 tests (p. 163).
One test = three specimens at different cell pressures (p. 163).

Recommended minimum number of tests for one soil stratum - to determine the effective angle of shearing resistance a: variability in strength envelope, coefficient of correlation r on regression curve; comparable experience none, medium, extensive: r ≤ 0,95 4, 3, 2; 0,95 << r ≤ 0,98 (as printed) 3, 2, 1; r ≥ 0,98 2, 1, 1; to determine the undrained shear strength a: variability in undrained shear strength (for same consolidation stress): ratio max/min values > 2 6, 4, 3; 1,25 < ratio max/min value ≤ 2 4, 3, 2; ratio max/min value ≤ 1,25 3, 2, 1. a One recommended test means a set of three individual specimens tested at different cell pressures (p. 163)

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Check triaxial cu against correlations with soil type and plasticity index, relating it to the test type; check φ' against correlations with soil type, plasticity and density index, adjust for in-situ stress conditions such as plane strain, and relate it to CPT results.
sections.body: (1) Besides a factual evaluation, check cu against correlations with soil type, plasticity index etc., and relate the evaluation to the type of test. (2) Check φ' against correlations with soil type, plasticity, density index etc.; consider laboratory and in-situ stress conditions (e.g. axi-symmetrical versus plane strain) and adjust φ' where relevant (p. 163); include relations with, for example, cone penetration test results and existing correlations (p. 164). (pp. 163 to 164)

Consider axi-symmetric versus plane strain for φ' (p. 163).

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Direct shear (box or ring) suits a distinct rupture plane or an interface; translational box and ring shear agree well, the box easier to prepare, the ring more homogeneous in stress and better for large strains and residual strength; take twice the material needed.
sections.body: (1) The direct shear (box or ring shear) test is preferably run where a distinct rupture plane is expected or interface strength is to be determined. (2) Comparative studies show good agreement between direct (translational) shear box and ring shear results; preparation is easier in the translational box; stresses are more homogeneous in the ring shear but strains are not uniform; large strains, and so residual strength, are easier to reach in the ring shear apparatus. (3) Take from the stratum twice as much material as needed for the number of specimens. NOTE: examples of procedures are in documents listed in X.4.4.4. (p. 164)
key_points: For a distinct rupture plane or interface strength (p. 164).
Ring shear better for residual strength (p. 164).
Take twice the material needed (p. 164).

More tests for settlement-sensitive structures (p. 165).

sections.title: Evaluation of compressibility characteristics
sections.summary: Compressibility comes from back-calculated settlements, empirical soundings, in-situ plate load and pressuremeter tests, or laboratory compression; back-calculation can be reliable, sand and gravel usually use field tests, mixed ground a combination, and laboratory tests suit fine and organic soil.
sections.body: (1) Four widely used methods: back-calculation of measured settlements; empirical evaluation of indirect in-situ investigations such as soundings; in-situ tests such as plate load and pressuremeter tests; laboratory compression tests. (2) Back-calculation from settlements under comparable stresses can be reliable (layered ground, load redistribution and time effects may be hard to allow for); for sand and gravel, field tests such as soundings are often used, interpreted empirically on comparable experience; where sands, coarser soil, silts and clays are expected, combine field and laboratory methods; laboratory tests are most reliable for fine and organic soil when quality class 1 samples are relatively easy to obtain. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.5. (p. 165)
key_points: Four methods: back-calculation, soundings, in-situ tests, laboratory (p. 165).
Sand and gravel: field tests interpreted empirically (p. 165).
Laboratory tests most reliable for fine and organic soil (p. 165).

sections.title: Detailed information on compaction testing of soil
sections.summary: Heading for Annex R, compaction testing of soil: procedures for both tests (R.1), Proctor compaction tests (R.2) and California Bearing Ratio tests (R.3).
sections.body: Annex R (informative) heading for R.1 to R.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 166)
key_points: See R.1 to R.3 (p. 166).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural guidance for compaction (Proctor) and CBR testing of 5.10.

sections.title: Test procedures applicable to both test types
sections.summary: At least three compaction specimens per stratum, the number set by engineering judgement from the variation of grading, consistency limits and quantity to compact; dams and roads may follow their own standards.
sections.body: (1) The minimum number of specimens for one stratum is three, the number specified based on engineering judgement. (2) Select the number considering the variation of particle size distribution, consistency limits and quantity of material to be compacted; for dams, road construction etc. it may be in the relevant standards. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.6. (p. 166)
key_points: At least three specimens per stratum (p. 166).
Dams and roads: number from relevant standards (p. 166).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural guidance for compaction (Proctor) and CBR testing of 5.10.

sections.title: Requirements specific to compaction tests
sections.summary: Standard and Modified (Proctor) compaction tests are most used; clean gravels and uniform coarse sands give no well-defined maximum density; stiff fine soil is shredded through 5 mm or chopped through 20 mm sieves; non-crushable soil may reuse one sample, crushable soil needs separate batches.
sections.body: (1) The most frequently used are the Standard and the Modified (Proctor) Compaction Tests. (2) Some highly permeable soils such as clean gravels, uniformly graded and coarse clean sands yield no well defined maximum density, so optimum water content may be hard to obtain. (3) For stiff fine soil, shred it to pass a 5 mm test sieve or chop it to pass a 20 mm test sieve. (4) Results then depend on the size of the pieces, and densities need not relate directly to in-situ densities. (5) Soil not susceptible to crushing may use one sample several times with progressively more water, the departure from common procedure being reported. (6) Soil with crushable particles needs separate batches at different water contents. (p. 166)
key_points: Standard and Modified (Proctor) tests (p. 166).
Clean gravels and uniform coarse sands: no well-defined maximum density (p. 166).
Stiff fine soil: 5 mm shredded or 20 mm chopped (p. 166).
Crushable particles: separate batches (p. 166).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural guidance for compaction (Proctor) and CBR testing of 5.10.

sections.title: Requirements specific to California Bearing Ratio (CBR) test
sections.summary: CBR: the laboratory test is definitive, on undisturbed or re-compacted material at the design moisture content, passing 20 mm with retained particles removed and weighed; not applicable if over 25 % by mass is retained; vary water after disaggregation without drying.
sections.body: (1) In-situ tests may be made, but the laboratory test is the definitive procedure. (2) Tests may be on undisturbed or re-compacted material. (3) Choose the moisture content to represent the design conditions (p. 166). (4) Test material passing the 20 mm test sieve, removing and weighing particles retained on it before preparing the specimen; if the retained fraction exceeds 25 % by mass of the passing fraction, the CBR test is not applicable. (5) For a range of water contents, add or remove water from the natural soil after disaggregation; the sample should not dry. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.2 (as printed) (p. 167). (pp. 166 to 167)
key_points: Laboratory CBR is definitive (p. 166).
Material passing 20 mm; retained particles removed and weighed (p. 167).
Not applicable if retained fraction > 25 % by mass (p. 167).
sections.applicability: Detailed procedural guidance for compaction (Proctor) and CBR testing of 5.10.

sections.title: Detailed information on permeability testing of soil
sections.summary: Heading for Annex S, permeability testing of soil: test procedures (S.1), number of tests (S.2) and evaluation of results (S.3).
sections.body: Annex S (informative) heading for S.1 to S.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 168)
key_points: See S.1 to S.3 (p. 168).
sections.applicability: Detailed minimum-test-count guidance and method-selection discussion for permeability characterisation of 5.11.

sections.title: Test procedures
sections.summary: Take twice the material needed, choose specimens representing the extremes of composition, density index and void ratio, keep the hydraulic gradient below 30 in clays and silts and below 10 in sand, and consider the degree of saturation needed.
sections.body: (1) Take from the stratum twice as much material as needed for the number of specimens. (2) Select specimens to represent the extremes of relevant properties, i.e. composition, density index, void ratio etc. (3) As a guideline the hydraulic gradient should be less than 30 in clays and silts and less than 10 in sand. (4) Consider the required degree of saturation according to soil type and required accuracy. NOTE: examples of procedures are in the documents listed in X.4.7. (p. 168)
key_points: Twice the material needed (p. 168).
Hydraulic gradient < 30 in clays and silts, < 10 in sand (p. 168).
sections.applicability: Detailed minimum-test-count guidance and method-selection discussion for permeability characterisation of 5.11.

sections.title: Number of tests
sections.summary: Table S.1 sets minimum permeability specimens per stratum by kmax/kmin and experience: 5, 4, 3 above 100, 5, 3, 2 from 10 to 100 and 3, 2, 1 at 10 or less; a single test verifies existing knowledge.
sections.body: (1) Table S.1 guides the minimum number of tests as a function of soil variability and comparable experience. (2) A single test in Table S.1 verifies existing knowledge; if results disagree with existing data, run additional tests. (p. 168)
key_points: kmax/kmin > 100: 5, 4, 3 specimens (p. 168).
tables: Table S.1: Permeability tests. Recommended minimum number of soil specimens to be tested for one soil stratum - variability in measured coefficient of permeability (k); comparable experience none, medium, extensive: kmax/kmin > 100 5, 4, 3; 10 < kmax/kmin ≤ 100 5, 3, 2; kmax/kmin ≤ 10 3, 2, 1 a. a A single test and classification tests to verify compatibility with existing knowledge (p. 168)
sections.applicability: Detailed minimum-test-count guidance and method-selection discussion for permeability characterisation of 5.11.

sections.title: Evaluation of test results
sections.summary: Permeability comes from field pumping and borehole tests (most reliable), grain size correlations (reasonable in homogeneous sand), oedometer tests (approximate; constant rate of strain better) or laboratory tests; give upper and lower limits; saturation and permeant chemistry can shift k by orders of magnitude.
sections.body: (1) Four widely used methods: field tests such as pumping and borehole permeability tests; empirical correlations with grain size distribution; evaluation from an oedometer test; laboratory permeability tests (p. 168); a combination can optimise the evaluation. (2) Even in a homogeneous stratum k can vary widely with small changes in stresses, void ratio, structure, particle size and bedding; field testing is the most reliable method. (3) Even in a homogeneous stratum describe k of a layer by upper and lower limit values. (4) For silts and clays, k from incremental oedometer results is only approximate; constant rate of strain oedometer tests measure it more directly. (5) In homogeneous sand k may be assessed reasonably accurately from grain size correlations. (6) For clay, silt and organic soil with high quality undisturbed samples, laboratory tests may be reliable, checking specimen representativeness. (7) For some soils the degree of saturation may change k by up to three orders of magnitude. (8) The permeant chemistry may change k by several orders of magnitude (p. 169). (pp. 168 to 169)
key_points: Field testing is the most reliable method (p. 169).
Give upper and lower limit values of k (p. 169).
Constant rate of strain oedometer more direct than incremental (p. 169).
Saturation can change k up to three orders of magnitude (p. 169).
